newsitem.title: UK: RTZ eases slightly after in line results.
newsitem.headline: RTZ eases slightly after in line results.

text.p: Shares in RTZ Corp Plc, the British arm of mining giant RTZ-CRA, eased five pence to 938-1/2 pence after the Anglo-Australian group released 1996 results which came in just as analysts had forecast.
"The share price is basically unchanged as the figures were very much in line with expectations," said one analyst.
Although the figures failed to excite, some industry watchers said they were pleased by the tone of the RTZ-CRA statement accompanying the results.
"The numbers were bang in line and the statement is positive," said Ian Rennardon at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
RTZ-CRA earlier reported 1996 adjusted earnings -- net profit after tax before exceptional items -- fell 24 percent to $1.096 billion.
One of the main reasons for the fall were operational problems with its major U.S. copper smelter in Utah. But RTZ-CRA said in its statement it saw major improvements taking place this year.
Later, at the company's news conference, RTZ-CRA said it expected the smelter's problems to be fixed by June. The problems to achieve full capacity cost the company about $150 million last year.
Also bolstering sentiment among analysts were RTZ-CRA's remarks that it saw good demand for its metals in coming years.
Nearly all analysts said they would leave their profit forecasts for 1998 unchanged. But Emile Morfett at Paribas Capital Markets said he planned to raise his estimates.
"It's a good set of results in a difficult year," he said.
"The resolution of the problems at Kennecott and what we're seeing at the moment in the aluminium and copper prices will see them post a fairly strong recovery," he added.
Aluminium and copper are RTZ-CRA's main metals. Prices for the two fell 22 and 16 percent respectively on average in 1996.
RTZ chairman Robert Wilson said the copper price fall was an overreaction to the trading scandal crisis triggered by Sumitomo trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
Copper and aluminium prices have picked up in recent months.
Wilson, meanwhile, called the copper market tight. He added he expected conditions to ease, although maybe only in 1998.
